lines: Fourteen. Where Do The Turkeys Go?.
So what happens after a pardon?
From 1989 to 2004, they went to Frying Pan Farm Park in Virginia.
Then things got glamorous.
In 2005, a turkey named Marshmallow, with his alternate, Yam, flew first class to California.
Marshmallow became Grand Marshal of the Disneyland Thanksgiving Parade.
His float said: "The Happiest Turkey on Earth."
In 2007, the pardoned pair went to Disney World.
Their names, May and Flower, were chosen in an online vote.
George W.

In 2012, Barack Obama's turkey Cobbler went to Mount Vernon, George Washington's home.
Full circle.

Democracy.
From 2016, the birds retired to "Gobbler's Rest" at Virginia Tech, for several years.

In case the first one can't perform.
Every year, a turkey trains for a job it hopes never to need.
And now the sad part.
These are farm turkeys, bred to be big.
A staffer at Frying Pan Park said they are "usually too fat and unhealthy to survive."
Many don't live long.
Pardoned.
But not immortal.
Fifteen. George W. Bush. Baghdad, 2003.
Thanksgiving 2003.
The United States had invaded Iraq eight months earlier.
George W.
Bush was believed to be at his ranch in Crawford, Texas.
He wasn't.
He'd flown secretly to Baghdad.
He spent about two and a half hours at the Baghdad airport, and served Thanksgiving dinner to about 600 soldiers.
Then came the photo.
Bush, holding a big, golden, perfect turkey.
And a rumor: the turkey was fake.
Plastic.
Not quite.
It was a real, cooked turkey.
But it was decorative.
A "trophy turkey," a standard feature of military holiday chow lines.
The troops were served from steam trays.
Officials said the President "picked up a decoration, not a serving plate."
So, real turkey.
Never eaten.
Technically, spared.
Scoreboard: we'll count it.

Every November.
Two birds, two names, one pardon, several jokes.
Donald Trump pardoned Drumstick in 2017, and Bread and Butter in 2019.
Joe Biden pardoned Chocolate and Chip in 2022.
Every year, the names sound more like a menu.
